title: Bloom Filters: how Cassandra answers exists queries without disk I/O

meta.yt_title: How Cassandra Answers Exists in 0.1ms Without Disk I/O (Bloom Filters Explained) #shorts
meta.yt_description:
How do high-performance databases know a record doesn't exist without scanning gigabytes of disk? Bloom filters.

• Bloom filters are probabilistic, memory-efficient bit arrays with k hash functions
• If any hashed bit is 0, the key definitely does NOT exist (0% false negatives)
• If all hashed bits are 1, the key might exist, triggering a disk lookup
• 1 billion keys need only ~1.2 GB of RAM for a 1% false positive rate

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: Burton H. Bloom (1970) CACM, Apache Cassandra Architecture.
meta.ig_caption:
How do Cassandra and RocksDB know a record doesn't exist in 0.1 milliseconds without touching disk? ⚡

They use Bloom Filters:

🔍 When searching for a key across millions of SSTables on disk, reading each file would destroy latency.

🧠 Instead, a compact bit array lives in RAM. The key is hashed with k independent hash functions.

🛑 If any bit is 0, the key DEFINITELY does NOT exist. Disk lookup skipped entirely!
✅ If all bits are 1, it might exist, so the database reads disk.

With just 10 bits per key, you get a 1% false positive rate and ZERO false negatives. 1 billion records fit in just 1.2 GB of RAM.

Follow @stackshade for more.

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: CACM 1970 Bloom Paper, Cassandra Docs.
